claim: Give every quantitative chart a visible value axis with labelled tick marks; if you strip the axis, put the value directly on or beside each mark instead.
why: Without a reference scale a bar's height is a shape, not a quantity — the viewer can compare bars to each other but cannot read any actual number.
when: Any chart whose purpose is to convey magnitudes: bar, column, line, area.
fails: Sparklines and inline trend indicators deliberately show only shape in a context where the exact value is stated nearby; there the axis is redundant furniture.

claim: Keep bar ends square, or at most round them by 2-4px. Do not round a bar cap by more than a few pixels of its width.
why: A heavily rounded top makes the bar's terminus ambiguous — the eye cannot tell whether the value sits at the apex of the curve or where the curve begins, so a decorative radius introduces real reading error.
when: Bar and column charts where the bar length encodes the value.
fails: Pill-shaped progress bars and capacity meters, where the fill is labelled with a percentage and the exact terminus carries no independent meaning.

claim: Match the number of marks in a chart to the number of real data points; never add extra bars, points or slices to balance the composition.
why: Marks are read as data. Inventing marks to fill space is fabricating data, and the viewer will try to map each one to a real category and fail.
when: Any chart built from a known dataset — especially mockups, placeholders and portfolio pieces, where the temptation to pad is strongest.

claim: When a chart's aesthetic treatment conflicts with its legibility, resolve in favour of legibility — accept the plainer version.
why: A chart exists to transfer a number to a reader; styling that impedes that transfer has cost more than it gained, however good the screenshot looks.
when: Reviewing or building any data display in a product interface.
fails: Purely illustrative or editorial graphics where the visual is decoration and no one is expected to read values off it.

claim: Do not use design-community shots (Dribbble, Behance and similar) as reference for charts; source chart patterns from analytics tools and charting libraries built for real data instead.
why: Portfolio shots are optimised to look good as a still image, not to be read, so they systematically drop the parts of a chart that make it legible.
when: Gathering visual reference before building a dashboard or reporting screen.

claim: Label the categorical axis with the actual categories, so a viewer can name what each mark represents without guessing.
why: A chart of seven weekdays should be readable as seven weekdays; unlabelled marks force the viewer to reverse-engineer the mapping, which is exactly where the padded-bar problem became visible.
when: Charts with a discrete category axis: days, months, cohorts, product lines.
fails: Dense time series where labelling every point is impossible; label at intervals and rely on a tooltip for specifics.

claim: Diagnose a weak dashboard as an information-architecture problem before touching visual styling — audit grouping, hierarchy, and density first, and only then adjust type, colour, and spacing.
why: The stated cause of failure is disorganisation rather than ugliness, so restyling a badly structured screen leaves the actual defect intact.
when: Critiquing or rebuilding a data-dense screen (dashboard, admin panel, analytics view) that feels wrong but has no single obvious visual flaw.
fails: The structure is already sound and the complaint is genuinely surface-level — contrast, alignment, or type scale — in which case structural rework is wasted effort.

claim: Build a dashboard by starting with the persistent navigation shell (sidebar) and working inward to content regions, rather than designing individual cards or charts first.
why: The navigation frame fixes the content area's available width and the page's top-level information hierarchy, so deciding it first prevents rework of every component sized against it.
when: Starting a dashboard layout from a blank canvas with no existing design system constraints.
fails: Working inside an established product shell where navigation is already fixed, or on a single-purpose view with no multi-section navigation.

claim: Hold a dashboard to three simultaneous criteria — structural simplicity, visual appeal, and real task usability — and treat a design that satisfies only appearance as unfinished.
why: The failure mode described is work that photographs well in a portfolio but does not support the user's actual job, so beauty alone is an insufficient acceptance test.
when: Setting acceptance criteria or self-reviewing a dashboard before shipping or portfolio publication.

claim: Give a dashboard one primary job and design the main area around it; if a new user would need training to read the screen, cut scope rather than rearrange.
why: Dashboards fail by accretion — every stakeholder's widget gets added until nothing reads as primary and the screen looks like dumped contents.
when: Designing or auditing the home/overview screen of an internal tool, admin panel, or SaaS product.
fails: Genuinely multi-purpose consoles where several workflows are co-equal; there you split into separate routes rather than forcing one job onto one screen.

claim: Use a smaller type scale with tighter steps for dashboards than for marketing pages — cluster body and label sizes closely (roughly 11–16px) instead of jumping across large display sizes.
why: A dashboard packs many more elements into the same viewport, so large type and wide size jumps waste space and break density; small, closely-spaced steps still create hierarchy at high information density.
when: Defining the type scale for any data-dense product UI.
fails: Landing pages and marketing surfaces, where few elements compete and large size contrast is the main hierarchy tool.

claim: Commit to a strict grid for dashboards and align every card and section to it; do not let modules free-float or use ad-hoc widths.
why: Dashboards fill the entire viewport, so any misalignment is visible against neighbouring modules — unlike a scrolling page where sections are seen in isolation.
when: Laying out the main content region of a full-viewport application screen.

claim: Put whatever the user's core job depends on in the top-left/primary cell of the main region — project status for a PM tool, holdings for a finance tool, the link list for a link shortener.
why: Placement in the main region is read as a statement of priority, so the top slot should map to the product's central object rather than to whatever data was easiest to chart.
when: Deciding module ordering in a dashboard's content area.

claim: Reserve the top strip of the dashboard for page-level actions and light navigation — typically one primary create button plus a filter or scope dropdown.
why: It gives actions a predictable, consistent home and separates 'things I can do' from 'things I'm looking at'.
when: Any dashboard or list view with a primary create action.

claim: Limit each row in a dashboard data list to about four or five fields: an identity marker, the primary value, its source or context, a timestamp, and one performance metric.
why: Rows are scanned, not read; every extra column reduces scan speed and pushes the layout toward a spreadsheet.
when: Displaying a collection of records on a dashboard home screen.
fails: Dedicated table/reporting views where users came specifically to compare many columns and expect column controls.

claim: Prefer a stacked, divider-separated list over individually bordered cards when showing many same-shaped records.
why: Each border is another visual line competing for attention; removing them lowers clutter while whitespace and dividers still carry the grouping.
when: Homogeneous repeated records where all rows have the same importance.
fails: Heterogeneous or independently-actionable modules, where borders correctly signal that each block is a separate object.

claim: If rows leave awkward vertical space, add a secondary metadata line (short description or context string) under the primary value rather than stretching or padding the row.
why: Filling the space with real information makes the density feel intentional and gives users a second way to identify a record.
when: List rows that look sparse at the chosen row height.
fails: When no meaningful secondary field exists — inventing filler text is worse than a shorter row.

claim: Design the empty state at the same time as the populated list, and let that requirement influence the layout choice.
why: A list container degrades gracefully to a single centered empty state; a grid of bordered cards leaves an awkward hole, so layout and empty state are one decision.
when: Any collection view that can legitimately have zero items — especially day-one for new accounts.

claim: Support multi-select on list rows and reveal a contextual bulk-actions control only once a selection exists, instead of showing bulk controls permanently.
why: Real accounts accumulate records faster than they can be managed one at a time, and a control that appears on selection teaches its own scope without adding permanent chrome.
when: Lists where users will realistically operate on many records at once (delete, archive, tag, export).

claim: Default to conventional chart forms — line for change over time, bar for comparison across categories — and reject novel or decorative chart shapes whose encoding a viewer can't name at a glance.
why: An unfamiliar chart form forces the viewer to decode the visual language before reading the data; the aesthetic gain never outweighs that cost.
when: Any analytics module inside a product UI.

claim: Ship every chart with gridlines and labelled axis values — these are the most commonly omitted elements and without them the chart shows only shape, not magnitude.
why: A trend line with no numbers can't answer 'how much', which is usually the question that sent the user to the chart.
when: All quantitative charts in a dashboard.
fails: Sparklines and inline trend indicators, where the shape alone is the intended message and the number lives adjacent.

claim: Pair each chart with a headline summary figure and a date-range selector in its header.
why: The summary answers the question without the user reading the plot, and the range selector makes the timeframe explicit rather than assumed.
when: Time-series and comparison charts on a dashboard.

claim: Use the same range-selector and metric-switcher controls across every chart on the page, and let users toggle between related metrics within one chart rather than adding a chart per metric.
why: Repeating one control pattern makes the whole module set feel like a system and keeps chart count — and therefore density — down.
when: Dashboards with two or more analytics modules.

claim: Identify rows in a categorical bar chart with the same visual token used elsewhere in the product (favicon, avatar, logo) placed beside the label.
why: A repeated identity marker lets users match a bar to a list row without reading text, tying the chart back to the data above it.
when: Bar charts broken down by an entity that already has an icon or image in the product.

claim: When designing an unfamiliar dashboard pattern, pull real shipped examples from a curated screenshot library first and study the flow, not just the surface styling.
why: Existing products have already resolved the hard structural problems — onboarding, settings depth, chart layout — and copying the structure is faster than rediscovering it.
when: Starting a dashboard or complex flow with no established internal precedent.
fails: Blindly matching visual style without checking whether the source product's constraints match yours.

claim: Pick the component for a field from the field's data characteristics — enumerable categorical values become chips/badges, quantities become right-aligned numerics, and long free text gets truncated with the full value available on demand.
why: The rendering then carries information about the data's nature, so a user can read type and constraint at a glance instead of parsing every cell.
when: Laying out any table or record list where columns differ in data type and cardinality.

claim: Right-align numeric columns and use a tabular/monospaced-figure setting so digits line up by place value.
why: Aligned place values make magnitude comparisons across rows a visual scan rather than a reading task.
when: Columns holding counts, currency, durations, or any comparable quantity.
fails: Numeric-looking identifiers (IDs, phone numbers, zip codes) are not compared by magnitude, so left-alignment reads better for them.

claim: Render a field as chips only when its value set is closed and small; free-text or high-cardinality fields should stay as plain text.
why: A chip visually asserts membership in a fixed set; using it for open-ended values makes the enclosure a lie and adds noise.
when: Status, department, employment type, role, tier — fields with a handful of known values.
fails: Applied to names, descriptions, or any field where the value set is unbounded; also breaks if the chip set grows large enough that colour coding stops being distinguishable.

claim: Truncate long text columns to a fixed width so the freed horizontal space goes to columns that need it.
why: One overflowing column otherwise dictates the whole table's proportions and squeezes everything else.
when: Tables containing a description, note, or address field alongside short structured columns.
fails: The truncated content is the primary thing the user came to read, or the truncation point hides the distinguishing part of the value.

claim: Encode row-level state in the row's own treatment — dim or desaturate inactive, archived, or deactivated rows instead of relying on a status column alone.
why: State becomes readable in peripheral vision, so users triage the list without reading a column.
when: Lists where a meaningful fraction of records are in a de-emphasised lifecycle state but still need to be visible.
fails: Dimming pushes text below contrast minimums, or the 'inactive' rows are the ones the user is actively working with.

claim: When a dataset's defining dimension is time, present it as a timeline rather than a table sorted by timestamp.
why: A timeline expresses interval and sequence structurally; a sorted table forces the user to reconstruct that structure by reading timestamps.
when: Event streams, activity feeds, audit logs, schedules — anything where 'when' and 'what happened next' is the question being asked.
fails: Users need to sort, filter, or compare across many non-temporal attributes, or the volume is large enough that scanning a timeline becomes slower than querying a table.

claim: Treat form factor and placement as separable — once data is re-formed into the right component, decide independently whether it lives in a sidebar pop-out, a secondary column, or the main area.
why: The right representation is a property of the data; where it sits is a property of the screen and the task priority.
when: Fitting a secondary view like a timeline or detail panel into an existing dashboard layout.

claim: Derive every colour in a dashboard from a data value, not from decorative intent; if you cannot name the field a colour encodes, remove it.
why: Dashboards are scanned repeatedly by the same users, so any colour that carries no meaning still consumes attention and dilutes the colours that do.
when: Choosing accent, status, and chart colours in data-dense product UI.
fails: Marketing pages, landing pages, and other low-frequency surfaces, where expressive colour serves a different purpose.

claim: Reserve high-salience colours such as red for rows or actions that genuinely require attention, and attach them to a small mark (an icon inside a chip) rather than flooding the row.
why: Salience is a fixed budget — spending it on urgency means the eye lands on the urgent item first without any reading.
when: Activity logs, audit trails, and alert lists where a minority of entries are urgent.
fails: Urgent entries are common, at which point the colour stops discriminating and everything reads as loud.

claim: Show identity with an avatar next to (or instead of) a name string in who-did-what columns.
why: Faces and image marks are recognised pre-attentively, so a user attributes an action faster than they can read and match a name.
when: Activity logs, comment threads, assignment columns, and any list where the actor is a recurring known person.
fails: Actors are unfamiliar or one-off, avatars are missing and fall back to identical placeholders, or the list has too many distinct people for recognition to work.

claim: Add a summary chart above a detailed list only when the data has a dimension worth rolling up — most often time — and let the chart answer the aggregate question the list would otherwise force the user to compute.
why: The chart converts a scan through a timestamp column into an instant read of trend or volume.
when: Logs, transaction lists, and event tables with a strong temporal or categorical aggregate.
fails: The chart is added as decoration over data with no meaningful aggregate, or the roll-up hides the individual records users actually need.

claim: Evaluate a dashboard revision by placing before and after side by side rather than judging the new version alone.
why: Improvements from alignment, density, and de-emphasis are relative and hard to see in isolation.
when: Iterating on data-dense layouts, in portfolio work as well as production.

claim: Delete any card, tile, or panel that has no interaction, no destination, and no data behind it, rather than leaving it as visual filler.
why: Non-functional surfaces teach users that clicking things does nothing, and they consume prime layout space that working controls should occupy.
when: Auditing a generated or inherited screen where some elements exist purely because a layout template called for them.
fails: The element is a deliberate empty state or onboarding placeholder that will hold real content once the user has data.

claim: Treat purely decorative, non-wired UI as a diagnostic marker of AI-generated screens and sweep for it as a first pass on any such page.
why: Generation optimizes for plausible visual completeness, so it reliably produces components that look interactive but are not connected to anything.
when: Reviewing a screen produced by a code-generation tool before shipping it.

claim: When one page holds two distinct concerns such as current consumption and payment/plan management, split them into tabs instead of stacking every section in a single scroll.
why: Tabs give each concern its own full canvas and let the user pick the task they came for instead of scanning past the other one.
when: A page's title covers two nouns joined by 'and', signalling merged responsibilities.
fails: The two concerns are consulted together in one glance, where tabbing forces the user to flip back and forth.

claim: Replace a row of identical plain-number stat boxes with a two-column layout that pairs each metric with a small chart such as a doughnut showing consumed versus remaining.
why: A bare number conveys magnitude but not position against a limit; a compact proportional chart shows how much headroom is left at a glance, which is the actual question on a usage page.
when: Displaying quota, credit, seat, or storage consumption where every figure sits against a known ceiling.
fails: The metric is unbounded or has no meaningful denominator, where a doughnut implies a limit that does not exist.

claim: Order pricing tiers so displayed prices increase monotonically down the list; if a discount breaks that ordering, show the original price struck through beside the discounted one.
why: Users read a tier list as a ladder, so a cheaper tier appearing above a more expensive one reads as a bug and forces them to reverse-engineer the discount before they can compare plans.
when: Presenting multiple subscription tiers where promotional pricing is applied to some but not all of them.

claim: Label every discounted price explicitly with the discount rather than showing only the reduced figure.
why: An unlabelled reduced price is indistinguishable from the tier's permanent price, so the user loses both the comparison anchor and the sense of urgency the promotion was meant to create.
when: Any tier list where promotional and standard prices appear side by side.

claim: Cap a pricing table at around three or four tiers; when there are five or more, merge or remove one, preferring to cut the weakest entry-level tier.
why: Each extra tier multiplies the comparison the user has to perform, and the lowest tier usually overlaps enough with a free plan or the next tier up to be redundant.
when: Designing or auditing a self-serve pricing page.
fails: Tiers map to genuinely distinct customer segments, such as an enterprise plan that cannot be folded into the others.

claim: When a page has multiple independent problems, rewrite it wholesale instead of patching each element in place.
why: Fixing components one at a time preserves the flawed underlying structure that produced them; restarting lets a coherent layout drive the component choices.
when: More than two or three sections of a screen fail review at the same time.
fails: The page is already in production and a full rebuild would break flows or links that currently work.

claim: Size type in a pricing card by decision weight, not by semantic rank: make the recurring price the largest element and demote the plan name to a small label.
why: Users scanning a billing page are comparing cost, not reading brand names for tiers; the element that drives the decision should win the visual hierarchy.
when: Pricing cards, plan selectors, and billing summary panels where the user is choosing or reviewing a paid tier.
fails: Contexts where the plan identity is the answer being sought — e.g. an account overview confirming 'which plan am I on', or a plan-comparison table where the name is the column header and the price repeats per row.

claim: When a layout gains horizontal space, spend it on hierarchy and added decision information rather than on stretching the existing elements to fill the width.
why: Extra width is a budget; scaling everything uniformly preserves the old hierarchy instead of improving it.
when: Refactoring a component after removing a sidebar, constraint, or nested container that was squeezing it.

claim: Before adding anything to a component, delete the elements that don't support the user's decision, then re-tune colour and size on what remains.
why: Subtracting first means the remaining hierarchy is applied to a smaller, higher-value set — otherwise you are tuning noise.
when: Any redesign pass on an existing, functioning component.

claim: If a user is on a discounted plan, display the actual saved amount as its own element, not just the discounted final price.
why: The savings figure is a benefit the product has already delivered; hiding it inside a net number means the user never perceives the value they're receiving.
when: Annual-billing discounts, promotional pricing, loyalty or volume pricing on a billing or checkout surface.

claim: On a current-plan card, list specifically what the next tier up includes that the current tier does not, rather than linking to a generic full pricing page.
why: An upgrade decision needs the delta, not the whole feature matrix; surfacing the gap in place removes a navigation step and makes the upgrade case concrete.
when: In-app billing settings where a user already has a plan and a higher tier exists.
fails: The user is on the top tier, or the tier difference is purely quantitative and already implied by a visible usage meter.

claim: Name pricing tiers to match the usage volume they actually serve — if a tier's quota implies an organisation of a given size, use the label that organisation would self-identify with.
why: A mismatch between the tier label and its limits makes users select the wrong plan or distrust the pricing; the name should be a shortcut to self-selection.
when: Defining or auditing the tier ladder for a usage-metered product.

claim: Treat a billing settings panel as incomplete until it shows the billing email and the payment method on file alongside the plan and price.
why: These are the details users come to billing to verify or change; omitting them forces a hunt through other screens for a routine task.
when: Account or workspace billing sections in a subscription product.

claim: Choose a tabbed settings shell when the product is expected to grow new capability domains, since each new domain becomes one additional tab with no restructuring of the existing layout.
why: The tab bar absorbs growth linearly; single-page or deeply nested settings require re-layout every time a new area appears.
when: Settings, account, and admin surfaces for products with a roadmap of additional feature areas (docs, integrations, AI, etc.).
fails: Settings surfaces with few, stable sections, or when the tab count grows past what fits in a single row and starts needing overflow behaviour.

claim: Don't ship a navigation slot you have no content for — when you add a tab or section, populate it in the same pass with the components it was created to hold.
why: An empty destination is a broken promise to the user and a signal the IA was drawn before the content existed.
when: Adding tabs, nav items, or panels during a layout redesign.

claim: Validate a novel UI pattern against how established products in the same category solve it before committing to it.
why: A widely used pattern carries learned user behaviour; matching it reduces the interpretation cost of your screen.
when: Designing conventional, non-differentiating surfaces such as pricing, billing, auth, and settings.
fails: Surfaces that are the product's actual differentiator, where copying the category norm forfeits the distinction.

claim: Prioritise the small, obvious features users expect over novel ones — they are cheap to build and materially raise how finished the product feels.
why: Perceived quality is driven by the absence of gaps in routine flows more than by the presence of standout features.
when: Deciding what to build next on an early-stage SaaS product.

claim: When a metric row represents an aggregate of several items, give it a toggle that expands into per-item series rather than forcing the user to a separate screen.
why: Users look at analytics to compare things against each other; an aggregate-only view hides the comparison they came for.
when: A dashboard chart or row rolls up multiple entities (links, campaigns, pages, channels) into one number or line.

claim: Place row-level action controls at the bottom of the row's content area rather than floating them above or beside the data.
why: Actions read as secondary to the data they operate on, so demoting them positionally lets the metrics own the top of the row.
when: A card or row combines a primary data display with a small set of controls or actions.
fails: The action is the row's primary purpose rather than an adjunct to the data, in which case burying it costs discoverability.

claim: Fill sparse dashboard rows with additional relevant metrics instead of leaving whitespace, and pair each metric with an icon that identifies it.
why: Analytics users tolerate — and want — density; icons let extra data points be scanned without adding text labels, and they introduce colour into an otherwise monochrome table.
when: A data row shows only one or two figures and the surrounding layout has unused horizontal space.
fails: The added metrics are not ones the user would act on — density for its own sake becomes noise.

claim: Use icons as a deliberate source of accent colour in data-heavy UI, not just as glyph decoration.
why: Dashboards default to grey text on white; small coloured icons break the monotony without requiring large colour blocks that would compete with the data.
when: A table, list, or metric row reads as flat and monochrome.

claim: For any metric that varies by geography, render a shaded choropleth map rather than a bar chart, and put the ranked numeric values in a panel beside it.
why: A map makes the spatial pattern legible instantly while the adjacent list preserves the exact values a bar chart would have given — the pairing beats either alone.
when: The dimension being charted is countries, regions, states, or cities.
fails: Only a handful of locations have data, or the user's question is strictly rank-ordering rather than spatial distribution — then the map adds visual weight without insight.

claim: Treat swapping chart types and adding icons as the highest-leverage first pass on a dashboard, before touching spacing, type, or colour tokens.
why: These two changes alter the perceived quality of the entire screen at a fraction of the effort of a full visual overhaul.
when: An existing analytics screen is functional but looks generic or auto-generated.

claim: Prioritise the landing page above in-product screens when allocating design effort on a SaaS product.
why: It is the surface where the most prospective users are lost, since they judge and abandon before ever reaching the app.
when: A SaaS product with a public marketing site and a signed-in application.

claim: Meet the established visual conventions of SaaS landing pages rather than inventing a novel presentation, because visitors read conformity to that standard as evidence of legitimacy.
why: Trust is assessed pre-consciously from surface quality; a page that misses the familiar standard reads as unserious regardless of the product's actual quality.
when: Designing a public-facing marketing page for a paid software product.

claim: Do not expect colour and layout fixes alone to make a landing page feel finished — budget for custom graphics or product imagery as a required element.
why: Correct spacing and palette only remove flaws; graphics are what supply the visual interest that distinguishes a designed page from a competently arranged one.
when: A landing page follows sound layout and colour rules but still reads as bare or templated.

claim: Generate cheap landing-page graphics by taking real product UI fragments — a card, a list item, a panel — and rendering them at a skewed or rotated angle as a decorative composition.
why: Skewing flat UI elements creates depth and implied perspective with no illustration or 3D work, and the fragments double as a product preview.
when: You need visual interest on a marketing page and have product UI but no design or illustration budget.
fails: Skew is applied to elements the user must actually read or interact with, where the distortion hurts legibility.

claim: Before redesigning a dense screen, count the discrete elements on it and state the number out loud; treat that count as the thing you are trying to reduce.
why: A specific count turns a vague sense of clutter into a measurable target and forces you to justify each item rather than accepting the whole grid as given.
when: Redesigning an existing dashboard, admin panel, or any screen with many parallel cards or widgets
fails: The element count is already low, or elements are genuinely independent — cutting to hit a number then destroys real functionality

claim: Temporarily hide persistent chrome (sidebar, nav, header) while auditing the content area, so you judge the content grid on its own before re-adding the frame.
why: Fixed chrome constrains and visually crowds the working area, making it hard to see the true shape and density of the content you're actually restructuring.
when: Early structural passes on an app screen where nav is stable and the content region is what's being redesigned
fails: The nav is itself in scope, or the content's proportions depend on the sidebar width you're about to change — you'll design to a canvas that doesn't exist

claim: Put a control inside the card for the object it acts on rather than giving it its own tile — a card-lock toggle belongs on the credit card card, not in a standalone 'system lock' widget.
why: A control separated from its target costs a whole container plus a label explaining what it applies to; co-locating it makes the relationship self-evident and reclaims the tile.
when: Any standalone widget that only ever operates on one other entity shown elsewhere on the same screen
fails: The control is global or applies across many entities, in which case it needs its own home

claim: Fold a derived or secondary metric into the card that holds the number it derives from — growth rate goes inside the annual-profits card, not beside it.
why: A percentage change is meaningless without its base value; pairing them makes each card a complete thought instead of forcing the eye to reassemble one figure from two tiles.
when: Dashboards where deltas, rates, comparisons, or trends are shown as separate tiles from their source metric
fails: The derived metric is the primary KPI for its own audience and needs equal visual weight

claim: Merge a chart into the card holding the metric it visualises rather than floating it as its own element, so one card carries value, change, and trend together.
why: A chart with no adjacent number and a number with no adjacent trend are both incomplete; combined they form a single self-sufficient unit and remove a container.
when: A chart on the canvas plots the same underlying quantity as an existing metric card
fails: The chart covers multiple metrics or needs large area for detail, where a dedicated full-width panel serves better

claim: If you cannot state what an element communicates within a few seconds of looking at it, delete it rather than redesigning it.
why: An element whose meaning is opaque to a designer studying it closely will be worse for a user glancing at it; polishing it spends effort on something that shouldn't exist.
when: Auditing inherited or client-supplied screens with legacy widgets of unclear intent
fails: The element is domain-specific and its meaning is obvious to actual users — check with them before cutting rather than assuming it's noise

claim: Cut bulky elements whose footprint is out of proportion to the value they deliver — a large survey or questionnaire block occupying prime dashboard space is a candidate.
why: Space is the scarce resource on a dashboard; an element's cost is the area it consumes, so value must be judged per unit of space, not in the absolute.
when: Large-footprint secondary content (promos, surveys, onboarding prompts) sitting alongside core metrics
fails: The bulky element is a business requirement or the screen's actual conversion goal

claim: When cutting something you're unsure about, remove it from the canvas now and note it as a possible re-entry later, instead of stalling the layout to solve it.
why: Keeping a doubtful element blocks structural progress; parking it preserves the option while letting the cleaner layout emerge and reveal whether it's still needed.
when: Mid-audit, when an element has some plausible value but no obvious home
fails: The parked item is a hard requirement — deferring it can produce a layout with no room to reinsert it

claim: Treat any structural fix as incomplete until you check the region it displaced; opening space in one area typically compresses or breaks another.
why: Layouts are zero-sum in a fixed viewport, so gains at the top are paid for below the fold.
when: After resizing, removing, or re-proportioning any major region of a fixed-height screen

claim: Consolidate before you style: resolve how many containers exist and what belongs in each one before touching type, colour, or spacing.
why: Visual polish applied to a wrong element count is wasted work, since merging cards later changes every size and spacing decision made before it.
when: Full redesigns where both structure and visual language are being changed
fails: Structure is fixed by an existing design system and only the visual layer is in scope

claim: Never show quantitative charts without labels or other context that lets users interpret the values.
why: Unlabeled numbers do not convey what is being measured or whether a value is meaningful.
when: A chart presents financial, performance, or other numeric data.
fails: null

claim: Remove a visualization when it repeats a metric that can be communicated more directly.
why: Duplicated information adds visual weight without adding decision-making value.
when: A chart mainly restates summary changes such as growth percentages.
fails: When the chart reveals trends, volatility, distribution, or comparison that the summary metric cannot show.

claim: Use compact metric chips to show percentage change at each relevant level of a hierarchy.
why: They make recurring growth values scannable without requiring a separate chart.
when: Users need to compare percentage changes across grouped dashboard entities.
fails: When users need to understand the time-based shape or causes of the change.

claim: Draw time-series data with clear, non-fading lines and avoid decorative curves that distort reading.
why: Curvature and fading reduce the clarity of the actual data path.
when: Displaying line charts where users must accurately follow values over time.
fails: null

claim: Provide gridlines, a time-scale control, comparison access, and a fullscreen route for an investment chart when those actions support deeper inspection.
why: These controls add interpretive context and let users inspect or compare portfolios without crowding the default view.
when: A dashboard includes a secondary chart that may sometimes need detailed analysis.
fails: When the data has no meaningful comparison target or detail view.

claim: Give lower-priority dashboard charts restrained visual emphasis and avoid allocating excessive space or interaction complexity to them.
why: Investment viewing and growth summaries are useful but may not be frequent core tasks.
when: The information is supplementary rather than central to the user's regular workflow.
fails: When monitoring investments is the product's primary user task.

claim: If a card's visual is pretty but carries no readable data point, delete the visual metaphor and replace it with a concrete event: a status icon plus the two or three facts a user would actually check (amount, date, location).
why: A dashboard card earns its space by answering a question at a glance; decoration that resolves to no fact is space spent on nothing.
when: Auditing dashboard modules where cards contain abstract diagrams, orbs, or charts with no labelled values.
fails: In brand or marketing surfaces, or hero areas where the visual's job is tone-setting rather than reporting.

claim: Start every alert card with a recognisable alert icon, then follow with the specific figures in descending order of what the user checks first (what happened → how much → when → where).
why: The icon does the categorisation instantly; the ordered facts let the user verify without opening anything.
when: Designing warning, fraud, security, or exception cards inside a status dashboard.
fails: When every card in a set carries the same icon — the signal stops discriminating and becomes ornament.

claim: Do not use a row of small unlabelled dots as the primary way to move between items in a data-dense module; use a labelled control that names the destination instead.
why: Tiny circles are both hard to hit and semantically blank — they tell the user neither where they are nor what they'd be moving to.
when: Any carousel, pager, or step indicator inside a compact dashboard card.
fails: Dots are acceptable as passive position indicators alongside a real navigation control, or in touch galleries where swipe is the actual mechanism.

claim: When an icon is too ambiguous or too large to survive at the size the layout allows, replace it with a text button rather than shrinking it further.
why: Shrinking a glyph past legibility makes both the meaning and the tap target worse; a word costs a little more space and removes the guesswork.
when: Header controls in modules where an icon must compete with a title and other affordances.
fails: Universally understood glyphs (close, search, settings) where the label adds nothing.

claim: Salvage a good graphic form from a failed card rather than discarding it — reorient it (e.g. rotate 90°) and re-tint it to fit its new content role.
why: The problem is usually the missing content, not the shape; reusing the form keeps visual consistency across the redesign and saves invention.
when: Redesign passes over an existing UI where some visuals are well-crafted but poorly applied.
fails: The form itself encodes a wrong relationship (e.g. a pie for non-part-to-whole data) — rotation and recolouring won't fix a wrong chart type.

claim: When a call-to-action button is the module's real purpose, promote it into its own module instead of leaving it embedded in another.
why: A primary action buried inside a secondary container is under-weighted relative to how often it's used.
when: Dashboard composition, once you've ranked which functions users hit daily.
fails: Promotions that fragment the layout — if the action has no supporting content to show, a button in place is enough.

claim: Let established module margins cap the item count in a new module: fit fewer, larger items rather than cramming more at the cost of consistent gutters.
why: Consistent internal spacing across modules is what makes a dashboard read as one system; per-module density exceptions break the grid.
when: Adding a module to a dashboard that already has a settled spacing rhythm.
fails: Content-heavy modules (tables, logs) where density is the point and a different, deliberately tighter spec is appropriate.

claim: Any module that shows only a truncated subset must ship with a visible 'view all' control, and if it accepts new entries, an 'add' control placed directly beside it.
why: Truncation without an escape hatch strands the rest of the data; pairing the two actions makes the module's full capability legible in one glance.
when: Preview modules — recent reminders, latest transactions, top alerts.
fails: The list is genuinely complete (a fixed set of three accounts), where 'view all' is a dead end.

claim: Rank modules by how often the underlying function is used day to day, and let that ranking drive size and vertical position rather than visual appeal.
why: Priority in a dashboard is expressed spatially; frequency of access is the most defensible proxy for priority.
when: Laying out or reordering a multi-module dashboard.
fails: Rare-but-critical functions (fraud freeze, emergency lock) that deserve prominence despite low frequency.

claim: Use a wide, short module shape for lists of short, homogeneous items with filters; reserve tall shapes for content that needs vertical scanning.
why: The aspect ratio should follow the item's natural reading direction — short reminder rows waste height in a tall container.
when: Choosing the footprint for a new list-type dashboard module.
fails: Long item lists where a wide-thin container forces excessive horizontal paging.

claim: Add filter controls at the point where a preview module shows fewer items than exist, so the two visible slots can be aimed at what matters.
why: With only a couple of slots, filtering is what makes the truncation useful instead of arbitrary.
when: Compact preview modules pulling from a larger dataset.
fails: Datasets small enough that filtering never changes what's shown.

claim: When a card holds numbers that split into opposing directions (in vs out, gain vs loss, before vs after), render them as a two-sided bar chart with one polarity above the baseline and the other below, rather than as two separate series or a plain number list.
why: The chart's geometry then encodes the semantics directly — direction reads as sign, so the viewer sees the in/out relationship before reading any label.
when: Paired opposing metrics over a shared time axis, e.g. revenue vs expenses per month.
fails: Categories aren't genuinely opposed, or one side dwarfs the other so badly that the smaller side collapses to invisible bars.

claim: Never let a data-bearing card be pure text and figures; give every quantitative module a visual representation of its data alongside the raw values.
why: Numbers alone force the user to compute trends mentally; a visual gives the shape of the data at a glance and the figures supply the precision.
when: Dashboard cards whose whole purpose is conveying a metric or a series.
fails: A single scalar with no comparison or time dimension — there's nothing to plot, so a large well-set number is the better treatment.

claim: Keep the exact numeric values on the card after adding a chart; the chart and the numbers do different jobs and should coexist.
why: Charts communicate relationship and trend but are imprecise; users still need the actual dollar figures to act on.
when: Any metric card where the precise value matters operationally.

claim: Give each embedded chart a small expand-to-fullscreen control so the compressed dashboard view can hand off to a detailed view.
why: A dashboard tile can only carry a summary; the affordance lets the summary stay small without truncating access to the full dataset.
when: Charts rendered at tile scale inside a grid of modules.

claim: Assign every module an explicit priority tier (high/mid/low) based on business importance, then lay the grid out by reading down those tiers — highest priority anchored at the top-left, mid next, low last.
why: Left-to-right, top-to-bottom reading order means grid position is itself a ranking; making the ranking explicit before placement stops layout from being decided by shape-fitting alone.
when: Composing a dashboard from independently designed modules.
fails: Modules with strong size disparities — a strict priority sort can force awkward voids, so priority sets the order and packing resolves the ties.

claim: When two arrangements of the same modules are both viable, choose the one that leaves no awkward residual gap — evaluate orientations by the shape of the empty space they produce, not just by how the filled blocks look.
why: A leftover region with an odd aspect ratio has no natural content that fits it, so it either stays empty or gets filled with filler that weakens the page.
when: Rotating or flipping a module pair inside a fixed grid.

claim: Treat a leftover gap in the grid as a prompt to ask what content the product is actually missing, and design a genuinely useful module for it — don't stretch existing cards or insert decoration.
why: Gaps usually reveal an incomplete information model; filling one with real missing content improves the product rather than just the composition.
when: Redesigns and audits, where the source design may have overlooked a whole category of information.
fails: There is no genuinely missing content — then whitespace or a resized module beats a padded-out invented card.

claim: Audit a domain dashboard against what a practitioner in that domain would need, not just against visual polish — a finance dashboard missing credit/liability information is incomplete regardless of how it looks.
why: Visual craft can't compensate for an information model that omits a whole dimension of the user's job.
when: Redesigning someone else's concept, or designing in a domain with established practice.

claim: Pick the chart type from the data's structure, and be willing to discard a first layout once a better-matching form occurs to you — proportional part-to-whole data (e.g. credit used vs available) belongs in a pie/donut, not a list or bar layout.
why: The right encoding makes the relationship self-evident; the wrong one buries it and forces label-reading.
when: Any module whose data expresses a share of a fixed total.
fails: More than a handful of slices, or when precise comparison between similar-sized segments matters — bars beat pies there.

claim: Cut secondary metrics off the face of a card and move them into a kebab/overflow menu rather than displaying everything the data source offers.
why: Card surface area is a ranking statement; showing a low-interest figure at the same weight as the primary one flattens the hierarchy, while the overflow keeps it reachable for the minority who want it.
when: A card whose dataset includes both a headline figure and supporting detail.
fails: The secondary metric is legally required, or is actually the number most users came for — hiding it then costs more than the clutter.

claim: Design each module in isolation first, then compose the page — don't fix the grid before the cards exist.
why: Card content determines its natural size and priority; deciding the grid first forces content to fit arbitrary boxes.
when: Multi-module dashboard work.

claim: Give every line chart horizontal gridlines and visible data-point markers before considering it finished; at minimum this is the baseline even in a small, space-constrained card.
why: Without a reference grid a viewer cannot estimate values, and without markers they cannot tell which points are real measurements versus interpolated path.
when: Any line or area chart plotting a continuous metric over time.
fails: Deliberate sparklines used as inline trend glyphs, where only direction matters and chrome would overwhelm the mark.

claim: Turn off curve smoothing (spline/bezier interpolation) on data lines; use straight segments between points.
why: Smoothing invents values between measurements and pushes the visual peak away from the actual data point, so viewers misread both the magnitude and the timing of highs and lows.
when: Charts where readers need to locate specific values or extremes on the series.
fails: Purely illustrative or marketing graphics where the line is a shape, not a claim about data.

claim: Do not fade, blur, or otherwise de-emphasise the most recent segment of a data series.
why: Recency is usually the highest-value part of the chart; visually softening it reads as hiding bad news and erodes trust in the product.
when: Time-series charts in financial, analytics, or health dashboards.
fails: The trailing segment is genuinely a forecast or incomplete period, in which case use an explicit dashed/labelled treatment rather than an unexplained fade.

claim: Add vertical gridlines aligned to time-axis ticks once the chart is large enough to carry them.
why: Horizontal lines let you read value; vertical lines let you read when — without them the time dimension is unanchored.
when: Charts scaled up enough that additional grid chrome does not crowd the plot area.
fails: Small charts where the added lines compete with the data line for attention.

claim: Delete an 'expand' or 'view larger' button when you can simply give the chart the space it needs in place.
why: A control that opens a bigger version of the same chart is compensating for a layout that under-serves the chart; fixing the layout removes the interaction entirely.
when: Dashboard cards where the chart is the primary content and space can be reallocated.
fails: Dense multi-widget dashboards where a genuinely larger, more detailed drill-down view exists and offers more than scale.

claim: Expose time-frame switching directly on the chart; lay the options out as a visible segmented row when space allows, and collapse to a dropdown only when it doesn't.
why: Visible options advertise the capability and make switching one tap; a dropdown hides both the current state and the alternatives, so it is a space-saving compromise rather than a default.
when: Any chart whose underlying data spans multiple meaningful ranges (day/week/month/year).
fails: Charts with a single fixed reporting period where a range control would imply options that don't exist.

claim: For business-performance metrics, plot the equivalent previous period as a secondary, visually subordinate line (e.g. neutral grey) behind the current series.
why: A single line shows movement but no baseline; the prior period turns 'up and down' into 'better or worse than last time' without the user doing arithmetic.
when: Revenue, sales, traffic and similar metrics where period-over-period comparison is the actual question.
fails: Absolute-value series like a stock portfolio balance, where the previous period is not a meaningful benchmark.

claim: Add a legend whenever the chart carries more than one series; skip it only if you can justify that the encoding is self-evident.
why: Two lines without labels force guessing; a legend is cheap, and the burden of proof is on omitting it, not on including it.
when: Multi-series charts, especially once a comparison line is introduced.
fails: Single-series charts, or where each line is directly labelled at its endpoint instead.

claim: Separate a chart's aesthetic quality from its functional quality when critiquing, and judge the function independently.
why: A chart can be beautifully styled and still fail its job; conflating the two lets polish disguise unreadable data.
when: Reviewing dashboards or any data-display UI.

claim: Diagnose a chart under its current size constraint first, then re-diagnose assuming the constraint is lifted — the two produce different fix lists.
why: Some problems are layout-budget problems, not design-taste problems; knowing which is which tells you whether to fix the chart or fix the page.
when: Improving charts embedded in fixed-size dashboard cards.

claim: Move the chart title out of the plot area's competing space and into a clear header position when you scale the chart up.
why: Extra plot space is only useful if the surrounding labels stop crowding it; repositioning the title is part of the same reallocation that grows the chart.
when: Rescaling a chart card within a dashboard layout.

claim: For recap content that users revisit to find or show a specific result, provide a fast scanning path instead of requiring one-step-at-a-time slide advancement.
why: Sequential slides make a first viewing feel curated, but impose unnecessary navigation cost when users want a particular statistic at a glance.
when: A product contains multiple personal stats or shareable milestones that users may revisit after the initial viewing.
fails: A strictly paced narrative is essential and users should not be able to skip ahead.

claim: Preserve a successful familiar format when redesigning it; improve the interaction model incrementally rather than replacing the whole layout.
why: Long-established user habits make a radical change riskier even when an alternative layout offers more functionality.
when: Refreshing a widely used, recognizable experience with meaningful existing user expectations.
fails: The legacy structure fundamentally prevents the core task or has no valuable learned behavior to retain.

claim: Use scrolling rather than discrete next-slide clicks for a recap that needs quick review across many items.
why: Scrolling lets users traverse and locate content more directly while still supporting an ordered recap sequence.
when: Content is arranged as a linear collection of recap moments, especially when people may browse nonlinearly after a first pass.
fails: Individual scenes require fixed timing, complex transitions, or deliberate acknowledgement before progression.

claim: Place recap navigation on the right edge and integrate it with a visible progress bar when the sequence includes video.
why: A combined control keeps orientation and progression in one persistent area while leaving the main canvas available for animated media.
when: Designing a scrollable, media-rich recap with a linear sequence and persistent navigation needs.
fails: Right-edge controls conflict with platform conventions, handedness/accessibility requirements, or important persistent UI.

claim: Organize a dense personal-data experience into a small set of named chapters, each centered on one user question such as favorite tracks, artists, mood, or change over time.
why: A clear narrative structure makes many statistics feel like a coherent recap rather than an unprioritized dashboard.
when: Designing an annual summary or any personal analytics flow with many possible metrics.
fails: Users need to compare many metrics simultaneously rather than consume a guided story.

claim: Keep expected headline metrics, then add a few distinctive secondary metrics that reveal behavior users would not normally notice.
why: Familiar metrics preserve recognition, while surprising details such as skipped content or late-night listening create delight and make the recap feel specific to the individual.
when: Refreshing a well-known recap format without losing its core value.
fails: The added metrics feel judgmental, inaccurate, or lack a clear user benefit.

claim: Frame artist statistics as changes over time or relationships, not only absolute totals.
why: Comparing this year with last year, identifying newly discovered artists, and showing one-track concentration gives raw listening counts a personal story.
when: Historical user data is available and the product is summarizing affinity, growth, or discovery.
fails: Prior-year data is absent, too sparse, or not comparable.

claim: Use an intuitive visual encoding for subjective qualities such as musical mood, and include historical comparison when the concept recurs annually.
why: A memorable color-based summary can make an abstract pattern legible; comparisons across years add meaning beyond a single snapshot.
when: Communicating an aggregate mood, style, or aesthetic signal in a recap.
fails: The mapping is too opaque for users to interpret or its visual output is inconsistent between periods.

claim: Choose recap metaphors that are immediately recognizable, compact, and easy to share without explanation.
why: Simple familiar symbols can turn a data summary into a playful social artifact.
when: Creating lightweight, shareable cards for broad audiences.
fails: The metaphor obscures the data, excludes part of the audience, or becomes more prominent than the insight.

claim: For a time-based listening journey, let users inspect every month rather than showing a selectively chosen subset.
why: Selective periods can feel arbitrary and prevent users from validating or exploring the story of how their taste changed.
when: The underlying behavior is naturally chronological and monthly data exists.
fails: The timeline is too long or sparse to browse efficiently without summarization controls.

claim: Prefer understandable category summaries over novelty-driven generated labels when users need to recognize themselves in the classification.
why: Personalization is only valuable when its categories are credible and interpretable to the person receiving them.
when: Presenting genre, identity, or behavioral segmentation in a consumer-facing summary.
fails: A generated label is transparent, controllable, and demonstrably more useful than standard categories.

claim: Group dense records by a meaningful retrieval attribute before adding space to every row.
why: More whitespace increases list length without resolving undifferentiated content.
when: Task lists or tables are hard to scan.
fails: Grouping can hinder comparison when users need a single stable ordering.

claim: Use recognizable avatars to distinguish people referenced in dense records.
why: Identity can be recognized without reading every name.
when: Users know the people and identity is relevant to the task.
fails: Unfamiliar or similar avatars still need readable names.
